text.en: Ikra and her little sister Samina have only one drawing sheet. Ikra wants to share it by cutting it in half, but Samina wants the bigger part. Ikra has a clever idea: she asks, would you like half of the paper or two quarters? Samina thinks two quarters sounds bigger. Is she right? In this chapter you will learn about halves, quarters, thirds and other fractions, and how sharing among more people makes smaller shares.

When an object is divided into two equal parts, each part is called a half. We write a half as 1 over 2. When an object is divided into four equal parts, each part is called a quarter, and we write it as 1 over 4. Both parts must be equal. If one part is bigger than the other, we cannot call them halves. Fold the paper and see whether the two parts fit exactly on each other. Samina thought two quarters was more than one half, but two quarters together make exactly one half. Ikra shared the paper equally. If we divide something into 5 equal parts, each part is one-fifth, written 1 over 5.
A rectangle can be folded into two equal parts in many ways: down the middle, across the middle, or along a diagonal. All of these give halves. There are also many ways to cut a rectangle into four equal parts, for example four strips, four small squares, or four triangles. Each part is one quarter. Equal parts need not look the same. They only need to be the same size. Two halves of a rectangle can be two rectangles or two triangles. To match a part with its whole, ask: how many such parts fit in the whole? If four of these fit, it is one-quarter. If two fit, it is one-half.
Sumedha's mother makes dhokla and asks the children to share it equally. Sumedha and Vinayak each get half. Two halves make a whole dhokla. When Kumar comes, the dhokla is cut into three equal parts, and each of the three children gets one-third. Three thirds make a whole. When Paridhi arrives, there are four people, so each gets one-fourth, which is one quarter. Four quarters make a whole. When Idha comes, five people share it and each gets one-fifth. The more people who share, the smaller each share. Idha does not like dhokla and gives her share to Sumedha. Now Sumedha has two pieces of one-fifth, which is two-fifths of the dhokla.
If a whole is shared equally among 2 people, each gets 1 over 2. Among 3 people, each gets 1 over 3. Among 4 people, 1 over 4. Among 5, 1 over 5. Among 8, 1 over 8. Among 9, 1 over 9. When the whole is divided into more equal parts, each part is smaller. One-ninth is smaller than one-eighth, and one-eighth is smaller than one-sixth. So Sumedha eats more dhokla if it is shared among 9 people than if it is shared among 11 people, because 1 over 9 is bigger than 1 over 11. Six pieces of one-sixth make a whole dhokla. Five pieces of one-fifth make a whole. This works for any fraction: if we have n equal parts and take all of them, we get one whole. Use the fraction kit to compare two pieces. The piece that is cut into more parts is the smaller piece.
Idha has seeds of five flowers: Rose, Mogra, Lily, Marigold and Jasmine. She plants them equally, so each flower gets one-fifth of the garden. She has very few Lily seeds, so she plants Roses in two parts. Now Rose has one-fifth and one-fifth, which is two-fifths of the garden. The other flowers still have one-fifth each. All the parts together still make one whole garden. If the garden is divided into 5 equal parts, we write the fraction for 2 parts as 2 over 5, which we read as two-fifths. The number below tells how many equal parts there are. The number above tells how many parts we take.
A fraction can be a part of a group of things, not only one shape. A box of 16 barfis is divided into four equal parts, so each part has 4 barfis. One-fourth of 16 is 4. Mohan's ribbon is one-fourth as long as Rohan's ribbon. That means Rohan's ribbon is four times as long as Mohan's. Think of other places where we use fractions: half a glass of milk, a quarter of a roti, one-third of a cake.
Fold a paper into 3 equal parts and colour one part. That is one-third. Fold it in half again and now there are 6 equal parts, and the coloured part is 2 of the 6, which is two-sixths. One-third and two-sixths are the same amount. If we halve the parts again, the coloured part is 4 of 12, which is four-twelfths. Notice that 1 over 3, 2 over 6 and 4 over 12 are all equal. Starting with one-half, we get 2 over 4, then 4 over 8, and these are equal to one-half. Two quarters make a half, and four eighths make a half. The fraction chart shows this: if you put two one-quarters under one-half, they fit exactly. Ten pieces of one-tenth make a whole. Three pieces of one-sixth equal one-half. Fractions that name the same part of the whole are called equal fractions.
Parts are equal only when they have the same size. When a square is cut into parts of different sizes, we cannot say each part is one-fourth. Sometimes you need to draw extra lines to make the parts equal before you can name the fraction. To name a coloured fraction, count the equal parts in the whole for the number below, and count the coloured parts for the number above.

problem.en: A whole is cut into 5 equal parts and 2 parts are coloured. Write the fraction.

text.en: Count the equal parts in the whole: 5.
Count the coloured parts: 2.
The fraction is 2 over 5, two-fifths.

problem.en: A box has 16 barfis. How many barfis are in one-fourth of the box?

text.en: Divide the barfis into 4 equal groups.

why.en: One-fourth means one of four equal parts.

text.en: 16 divided by 4 = 4.
So one-fourth of 16 is 4 barfis.

problem.en: Is one-half the same as two-quarters?

text.en: Fold a paper into halves and shade one half.
Fold it again to make 4 parts: the shaded half covers 2 parts.
So 1 over 2 equals 2 over 4.

why.en: They name the same part of the whole.

points.en: A half is one of two equal parts, a quarter is one of four equal parts.
The more equal parts a whole is divided into, the smaller each part is.
Fractions of a collection: one-fourth of 16 is 4.
Equal fractions, like one-half and two-quarters, show the same amount.
